extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of moral philosophy; authors of personal/self-reflective essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles embedded in a Montaigne-style personal essay about virtue, conscience, and repentance — i.e., how to judge actions and how to practise/describe repentance and private virtue. Useful for readers assessing moral behaviour or writers of self-reflective philosophical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public utility does not justify private immorality
rubrics_metrics.description: “No private utility is of such importance that we should upon that account strain our consciences ... the public may be, when very manifest and of very great concern.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow exceptional public-utility justifications only in very manifest, very great cases; be mindful of the danger of example (bad precedents). Example: Timoleon’s act had mitigating factors (tears, fraternal claim) and was judged cautiously because of the danger of the precedent it set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply dangerous exceptions with moderation and circumspection
rubrics_metrics.description: When an action is a dangerous or exceptional model (e.g., killing a relation for public good), yield only with great moderation and circumspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an end might be excused (e.g., public deliverance), decisions must weigh the risk of corrupting example; political bodies may rightly defer judgment or refer to less-partisan evaluators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer judgment when interested parties are conflicted
rubrics_metrics.description: When those most concerned cannot judge impartially (e.g., Syracuse divided about Timoleon), it is proper to discharge their judgment and refer the matter to others less concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation reduces bias and the danger of self-justifying precedents; the Senate’s refusal to decisively condemn Timoleon illustrates prudent deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths under duress remain obligations unless the promise was unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: If fear once made me willing to promise (e.g., to robbers), I am obliged to keep my word when no longer in fear — except when the promise itself was unlawful or wicked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne rejects the easy excuse that duress absolves all promises; distinguish coercion that only affected speech from genuine invalidity (e.g., promises to commit wicked acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private rights persist amid public dissension
rubrics_metrics.description: “The memory of private right remaining even amid public dissensions” — private claims and duties do not vanish simply because of public quarrels or war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public necessity does not automatically trump family obligations or private justice; cite classical authorities (Livy, Ovid, Cicero) to support that some private duties remain binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: True repentance must be deep, universal, and affect the whole conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance is not superficial or partial; 'I know no repentance, superficial, half-way, and ceremonious; it must sting me all over ... and must prick my bowels as deeply and universally as God sees into me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere dissatisfaction or wishing to be better from authentic repentance; genuine repentance requires comprehensive internal change and pain proportionate to the wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repentance only concerns what is within our power; sorrow is different
rubrics_metrics.description: Wishing to be other than one is (or envying a nobler nature) is not repentance; repentance properly addresses things under our control, not merely desire or regret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count moral self-reproach about limitations beyond one’s power as true repentance; measure repentance by attainable corrections in conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge virtue by private, ordinary behaviour rather than public deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue of the soul 'does not consist in flying high, but in walking orderly' — private duties (paying, loving, conversing gently with family) are harder and more telling than grand public exploits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral character by everyday conduct at home and in ordinary situations; public fame can be misleading because it highlights rare acts rather than consistent disposition (Socrates vs Alexander comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use one’s own conscience as primary judge, not public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: “You yourself only know if you are cowardly and cruel, loyal and devout ... rely not therefore upon their opinions, but stick to your own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form an internal standard and test actions against it; public praise and reproach are unreliable guides for one’s moral self-assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic piety/devotion requires matching change in life; outward show is easy
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion is 'abstruse and occult; the appearance easy and ostentatious' — piety is easy to counterfeit unless the person conforms manners and life to profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religious or moral professions by observable, sustained life-changes rather than by ceremonies or statements alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual, will-rooted sins resist sudden repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sins that have been long rooted in a vigorous will are not subject to quick recantation; sudden claims of complete reformation are hard to credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate impulsive, momentary sins (which can be disowned) from entrenched habitual vices; genuine reformation of deep habits requires sustained alteration, not a single emotional resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish error of judgment from misfortune — do not repent for unforeseeable outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: If prudent counsel was followed but events turned contrary due to hidden conditions or fortune, one should not repent of the council ('I do not repent that I counselled the other') — blame fortune, not reasonable judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing past decisions, separate flaws in deliberation from unforeseeable contingencies; moral self-reproach should target failures of judgment, not unlucky outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private conduct reveals settled nature better than public performances
rubrics_metrics.description: People are better judged when 'at home, whenever that may be; and, at all events, when they are nearer repose, and in their native station.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe how a person behaves away from spectacle to infer their durable character; public roles and staging may mask true disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural inclinations are persistent and may be concealed but not easily eradicated
rubrics_metrics.description: Original qualities are not to be rooted out; they may be covered and concealed — nature can reassert itself (e.g., Latin words returning under emotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that deep inclinations will resurface under stress; evaluate claims of permanent change accordingly and be cautious in promising wholesale transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base virtuous action solely on others’ approbation
rubrics_metrics.description: To ground the recompense of virtuous actions upon the approbation of others is 'too uncertain and unsafe a foundation' — public opinion is corrupt and unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate virtue for its intrinsic worth and for one’s conscience rather than to secure public praise; otherwise moral action becomes contingent and hollow.
